newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK's unions back single European currency.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK's unions back single European currency.

text.p: Britain's trade unions threw their weight behind a single European currency on Tuesday and urged UK politicians from both major political parties to do the same.

John Monks, general secretary of the unions' umbrella body the Trades Union Congress (TUC), told a conference here on European Monetary Union (EMU) that Britain's "wait and see' approach to the single currency was increasingly untenable.
"The option of commitment to joining the first tranche of EMU membership is the one which, on balance, the TUC favours because the risks of the alternatives are too great," he said.
The single European currency, or euro, is scheduled to start on January 1, 1999.

Monks' comments may cause a stir within the opposition Labour party, the unions' traditional ally, which, like the Tory government, has said it will wait until the 1999 deadline for the euro is closer before deciding whether to join EMU.
Both political parties are tiptoeing carefully through the EMU minefield, scared of of alienating a sceptical British public ahead of general elections to be held by May.
Monks said that by dithering over EMU, the UK was in danger of missing out by default on what he termed the most important economic development in Europe since the war.
Peter Sutherland, chairman of U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs and former Director-General of the World Trade Organisation, also endorsed Britain's entry to EMU.
"Britain is vitally important for Europe just as Europe is vitally important for Britain," Sutherland told delegates at the conference organised by a European think-tank.
He said any postponement of a single European currency would be extremely dangerous. "I don't think delay is a real option."
Sutherland, a former European Commissioner, said British industry and businesses would lose out if excluded from EMU, possibly being forced to pay premium interest rates.
The TUC endorsement of EMU is the latest in a series of squabbles with the Labour Party, centring on the Party's historic ties with the labour movement.

Labour said last Sunday it would hold a referendum before taking Britain into the European Union's planned single currency. The move brings the opposition into line with the ruling Conservatives, who promised in April to hold a plebiscite on the issue.
Monks argued that exclusion from EMU would hold more dangers for Britain than inclusion and would be disastrous over time.

He said Britain would have higher interest rates than Europe, would see a steady reduction in trade with the rest of Europe and would risk losing the inward investment that has been such a significant economic boost in recent years.

Inclusion, on the other hand, would promote stable economic conditions to stimulate growth, boost employment and trade and foster a stable currency regime with significant cost reductions, Monks said.

He added the timetable for the first wave of entry to EMU was such that unless the new government's attitude toward EMU is clear shortly after the 1997 general election, the option of early participation will disappear.
"The UK will simply not be able to participate," he said.
